d.title: Three branches finished and their results went with the failing one
d.caption: **And that is correct, not a flaw: a superstep is a transaction — either all of its writes commit or none do — because committing a partial superstep would leave state no node had agreed on.** It is the same property that makes 14.3's retry transparent, where a failed attempt leaves no trace. **Correct, and the exact opposite of what partial results need, which is why k-of-N is not a configuration setting.**

d.title: A threshold, not whatever arrived
d.caption: The same 3 of 5 passes at k=3 and fails the run at k=4, **which makes it a product decision rather than a tuning knob.** And the label is the rest of it: **a run that answers from 1 of 5 sources and does not say so is worse than an error, because the user cannot tell the answer is partial and will act on it as if it were complete.** *“I could not reach the billing system, so this excludes your balance”* **is a degraded answer; the same text without the caveat is a wrong answer. That sentence costs one string.**

d.title: Four calls, and the fifth was never made
d.caption: **The check belongs in the router, before the next call — checking afterwards tells you that you have already overspent, which is a report rather than a budget.** And **it exits through a node that produces something, not by raising: a budget that raises has spent the money and thrown away the work, the worst of both.** The exhausted run returns its partial answer, labelled — the same rule as the k-of-N case.

d.title: A recursion limit for structural loops, a call budget for semantic ones
d.caption: **A loop that is making progress by LangGraph's reckoning never hits the recursion limit — and that default is 10007 supersteps, which at $0.012 a call is roughly $120 before anything stops it.** So the call budget is the much smaller number and the one that catches a silent loop. **All three belong in the config and are read in the router, which also makes them testable without reaching into the graph.**

d.title: The exception is the smallest part of what survives
d.caption: **Three fields carry the weight: `next` names the step that failed, the completed list says what already happened, and the `checkpoint_id` is what makes resuming possible at all.** One detail worth knowing: **the error is stored as a string, not an exception object — so a dead letter can report the failure but cannot re-raise it**, which is fine for a human and matters if you meant to branch on the exception type during an automatic drain.

d.title: Two fields nobody thinks of, and both must be written when the step ran
d.caption: **`effects_already_applied` tells the human the card is charged before they decide anything — without it they have to go and look, and under pressure they may not, which is how a refund gets issued twice or a shipment goes out for a cancelled order.** `compensation_handles` is 14.4's point: *“refund the card”* is not actionable and *“refund `txn_8841`”* is. **Both have to be captured when the step ran, because the system that would tell you later may be the one that failed.**

d.title: Only the failed step executed, so the card was not charged twice
d.caption: **This is the property that makes a dead letter queue safe to drain automatically — and it depends on the call form: 10.8 measured that `invoke(input, cfg)` starts a new run and only `invoke(None, cfg)` resumes, so a drain written with the obvious call signature repeats every effect.** And **a queue whose entries can only be re-run from the start is a queue you dare not drain — so it fills up, nobody touches it, and it becomes a list of things nobody did.**

d.title: Alert on the age of the oldest entry, not the depth
d.caption: **A depth of 3 that is four days old is worse than a depth of 40 that is five minutes old: depth measures arrival rate, age measures whether anyone is acting** — and the second is the actual failure mode. Both killers are organisational: **no owner makes it a log file with extra steps, and no classification makes 500 entries of one cause read as 500 problems.** The metric for the mechanism itself: **what fraction of dead letters a human resolved by an action that could have been automated.**

d.title: Three aggregates for a system where one run guessed and one did triple the work
d.caption: **Exact-match trajectory scoring has the worse problem: it assumes one correct path, and for most questions there are several — so a perfectly good alternative route scores zero, which makes the metric fight any improvement to the agent's planning.** And it marked run 3 down for being **inefficient rather than wrong**: the right signal in the wrong column, because efficiency is worth measuring and should not come out of the correctness score.

state: the guess, and the triple call

d.title: Three measurements, and each verdict maps to a different fix
d.caption: **“Right answer, wrong source” justifies trajectory scoring on its own: it is indistinguishable from success on every output-based metric — exact match, BLEU, an LLM judge, a human reading the answer. All of them see a correct response.** And it is the failure that **generalises worst**: right on your test set and wrong in production, **because the mechanism that produced the right answer was not the mechanism you intended.** 7.1's lesson — a plausible path to the right output is not evidence the path was used.

d.title: Most agent evaluation is outcome-only because the labels do not exist
d.caption: Each case needs the question, the expected answer, **and the set of tools a correct answer requires** — and that last field is expensive: **it means someone deciding, per question, which sources a correct answer must consult.** Not that trajectory scoring is disputed; the labels simply are not there. **The cheap approximation is one line per case: assert that certain tools must appear and certain tools must not.** *“Must call `get_order`, must not call `search_web`”* catches run 2 without labelling a path.

d.title: Five metrics that need no labels and catch real bugs
d.caption: **None of these tells you whether the answer was right, and all of them tell you something an outcome score cannot** — so they are worth having **before** a labelled set exists, which is the order most teams end up in anyway and not a compromise. The tool-error row is the bluntest of them: **a tool failing 40% of the time is a dependency problem wearing an agent costume.**

d.title: Seven attributes, none of them present by default
d.caption: **The attempt number is the one that silently corrupts metrics: 14.3 measured a node running three times inside one successful run, so without it p99 latency and cost per run are both wrong — and a duplicate-call detector fires on retries that were working exactly as configured.** Which is a general shape: **the retries, fallbacks and degradations are all invisible successes, and they all distort the numbers you use to judge the system.**

state: a failure maps to no conversation

d.title: Six calls, two distinct pairs, and the run succeeded
d.caption: **This run finished, answered, and never came near the recursion limit — which defaults to 10007 supersteps, so a loop making two calls a turn is nowhere close. The only signal is the repetition.** So: **count distinct `(tool, arguments)` pairs per run against the total. The ratio is near 1.0 for a healthy run and falls as a loop develops.** It needs no labels, no gold answer and no model call — **a group-by over the trace, which is why it is the first metric to add.**

d.title: Three levels, and one thing not to log at any of them
d.caption: **Not the full prompt on every span: it is the single largest thing you could log, it grows quadratically with the conversation (13.1), and it contains whatever the user typed — so the storage cost and the privacy exposure both scale with exactly the sessions you most want to keep.** The working compromise: **a hash plus the token count always, and the full prompt only on failures or a sample. A reported failure is then almost always in the sample, and a working run costs a hash.**

d.title: Work backwards from one question
d.caption: *“A user says it was wrong at 14:30 — what happened?”* **Answering needs the `thread_id` from their session, the run within it, the span tree, the tool arguments and results, and the prompt as it was actually sent. If any of those is missing, the answer is a guess** — **and the last one is usually what is missing**, for the good reason above. **Designing from that question rather than from a list of metrics is what stops you collecting five dashboards that cannot answer it.**

d.title: Calls per unit of work, which is the budget difference at volume
d.caption: **A choice made for clarity — split this into a supervisor and two workers — is also a decision to spend 67% more model calls per unit of work. That is a defensible trade and it should be made knowingly.** And **plan-and-execute is the outlier worth remembering: its workers have a constant prompt (13.6), so 13.1's quadratic growth never reaches them** — the one pattern that scales to an arbitrarily long task with none of module 13's machinery.

d.title: Sixty-five percent on a cache that can never be wrong
d.caption: Real traffic is **Zipfian** — a few questions dominate, so 100 queries held only 37 distinct ones. **And an embedding is a pure function of its input, so this cache can never serve a wrong answer: cache it forever, keyed on (text, model, model version).** The version in the key is the only subtlety, **and omitting it means a model upgrade silently mixes two vector spaces** — which makes this the best cache in the stack: cheap to verify and impossible to serve incorrectly.

d.title: Four things you might cache, and one of them is a breach
d.caption: **A model response is cacheable only for identical prompts — and 13.1 means the prompt contains the whole history, so two users never share one: the hit rate is near zero outside tests.** The last row is not a performance question: **7.5's finding is that a cache keyed on the question alone will serve one user's filtered results to another**, which is a data breach produced by a performance optimisation, and it passes every single-user test.

d.title: The limit has to be where the scarce resource is
d.caption: The provider rate limit saturates first, **because the model call is ~80% of the turn and the only part you do not control** — so **the concurrency limit that matters is on model calls and belongs in front of them, not at your HTTP layer. An HTTP limit of 200 against a provider limit of 20 means 180 requests racing to discover a 429, each after paying for retrieval and reranking.** What to watch, in order: queue depth, 429 rate, cost per run, p99 turn count, **and the retrieval index's memory — the only non-model component that genuinely saturates, and it does so suddenly.**

d.caption: **All four fail silently and pass single-user testing**, which is what puts them in their own section. d.title: A checklist is the only instrument that catches a missing detector
d.caption: No version pins, no deployment topology, no model choice — **those change faster than the failure modes do, and every item above survived the 1.x rewrite that moved `config_schema` to `context_schema` and relocated `default_retry_on`.** Every item has the form *“a mechanism exists for X”*, **because this course's findings are nearly all of the form “X fails silently and nothing tells you” — 14.1 counted five of nine surfaces as silent. A test suite verifies the behaviour you thought of; a checklist asks whether you thought of it.**

d.title: The zeroth item, and every other item is a cost of answering it yes
d.caption: **11.1 and 12.1 reached the same answer from different directions: a chain is cheaper, faster and debuggable, and a multi-agent system costs coordination calls per unit of work. So the real first question is whether the control flow is genuinely data-dependent at runtime — and if the steps are known in advance, a chain does it with one model call and none of the five sections apply.** Which is not an argument against agents: **the list is long because the capability is genuinely powerful and genuinely expensive to operate.**
